title: How 100 Starlings Took Over a Continent, and What They Teach Us About Evolution
summary:
In the late 1800s, a bird lover named Eugene Schieffelin released about 100 European starlings in New York City's Central Park. He was chairman of a group that wanted to bring plants and animals from Europe to North America. The plan worked far too well. Within decades, the starlings had spread across the whole country. By 1970, less than a century after their arrival, there were 200 million of them.

That explosion makes starlings a puzzle for scientists. How did such a small group of birds adapt so quickly to so many different places? Part of the answer may lie in microevolution, the small changes that build up within a species over time. When a new population starts from just a few birds, it carries only a small sample of the original group's genes. Scientists call this the founder effect. It can reduce genetic variety, yet starlings still managed to adapt fast to local climates across North America.

Researcher Zichello wanted to measure how the birds had changed. In 2014, she asked the U.S. Department of Agriculture for starling specimens for her research, and five birds arrived in a box labeled Honey Baked Ham. Wildlife agencies remove starlings each year to protect crops and keep planes safe, and about two million are killed annually by the USDA. Zichello used her five birds to study tiny differences between individuals, in their anatomy and in their DNA, to understand how the species changed after its dramatic start.

Starlings in a flock look almost identical, like glossy little soldiers marching through the grass. But measuring small differences, bird by bird, can reveal how evolution works in real time. As Zichello puts it, her box of birds was evolution in a garbage bag.
why_it_matters: Starlings show how quickly living things can change when they move to a new home, which matters for protecting crops, wildlife, and the balance of nature.

keywords.explanation: Microevolution means the small changes that slowly build up inside a species over time.

Specimens are single animals kept for scientists to study closely.
Anatomy is the shape and structure of a living thing's body and its parts.
Glossy means shiny and smooth, like a polished surface.

background_read: Starlings are small, dark, glossy birds that live in large flocks and are now common across North America.
Evolution is the slow change of living things over many generations, as small differences help some individuals survive and have more young.
When people move a species to a new place, the newcomers can spread fast if they find food, shelter, and few enemies.
Scientists study DNA, the instructions inside living cells, to trace how populations change over time.
